LESSON 11 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

TCP, UDP and the Three-Way Handshake

What TCP and UDP each promise, how the three-way handshake sets a connection up, and what ordering, retransmission and connection state mean for a defender.

Beginner15 min
Why this matters

TCP and UDP are the two transport protocols most traffic uses. TCP sets up a connection and guarantees ordered delivery; UDP sends without either. Choosing between them is a security decision as much as a performance one.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A TCP connection starts with a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, then ACK, which agrees sequence numbers and options before data flows.
  • TCP numbers bytes, retransmits what is lost, and reassembles in order, so the application does not deal with duplicates or gaps.
  • TCP also closes politely, which is why a connection can sit half-open and consume resources if the final packet never arrives.
  • UDP sends datagrams with no setup and no guarantee of delivery or order, which makes it simple, fast, and easy to spoof.
  • A modern application over UDP may still add its own reliability layer, so the transport choice does not by itself tell you how reliable the data is.

The background

  • TCP was designed for a lossy network to make reliability a feature of the transport rather than every application.
  • UDP came from the same era as a deliberately minimal option for cases where the application preferred to handle its own guarantees.
  • The handshake that establishes a connection is also what made TCP scans an early reconnaissance technique.
  • QUIC builds reliability and encryption on top of UDP to avoid head-of-line blocking, and browsers now prefer it where supported.

Real-world examples

  • A SYN flood consumes resources in the half-open state, which is why the operating system keeps a queue of them.
  • A UDP amplification response is much larger than the request, so a small amount of traffic becomes a large one.
  • Some malware uses TCP as well as UDP for command and control, so blocking one protocol is not sufficient.

What to look for

  • Check whether a service really needs to be reachable over UDP as well as TCP.
  • Rate limit connection attempts, not just bandwidth.
  • Look for services that respond more quickly than they should, since a short response is often a reflection or amplification surface.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Keep connection-state tables bounded and aged out so half-open connections cannot accumulate.
  • Filter unsolicited UDP at the edge, since most internal traffic is not inbound UDP.
  • Rate limit by source address, and consider source validation for UDP you must expose.
  • Alert on connection-rate anomalies rather than only on volume anomalies.
